adults.title: Strength Built a Day at a Time
adults.big_idea: Small and simple things—scripture study, prayer, the sacrament, and covenants—build a spiritual immunity that gives us strength and courage in Jesus Christ to withstand the challenges of life.
adults.objective: Learners will name the burden they most need strength for and choose one small and simple practice to do daily this week, trusting the Lord to strengthen them.
prepare: Read Elder Christian C. Chigbundu's talk, Spiritual Immunity (Saturday afternoon session). Mark paragraphs on scripture study, prayer, the sacrament, and covenants.
Write four headings on the board: Scripture study, Prayer, The sacrament, Covenants.
Bring slips of paper and pens for everyone.
Ask class members to open the talk in Gospel Library as they arrive.
Pray by name for those you teach; ask to know who is carrying a heavy load.

segments.name: What weighs on you?
steps: After the opening prayer, give everyone a slip of paper. Explain that Elder Chigbundu asked his listeners a question, and you will ask it too.
Read the question aloud, then allow one full minute of silence for people to write an honest answer. Tell them no one will see it.
Ask them to fold the slip and keep it in their hand or their scriptures. The rest of the lesson is about that slip.

Briefly set the scene: during the health crisis of 2020, health professionals who spoke at Elder Chigbundu's workplace kept returning to one word, immunity—the body's ability to defend and protect itself. He found himself thinking about what he calls spiritual immunity.
questions: What keeps you awake at night or weighs on your mind?

segments.name: Immunity is built, not wished for
steps: In pairs, take one minute: What ordinary things keep a body able to fight off illness? Hear three or four answers quickly and point out how small and repeated they are.
Ask someone to read the first key quote (T11.04). Note that Elder Chigbundu names wars, family challenges, and economic uncertainty, and still says we need not fear.
Read Alma 37:6 together. Explain that Elder Chigbundu calls these small and simple things a spiritual compass the Lord has provided.
Ask the question below and let two or three people answer.
questions: Why do you think the Lord so often chooses to strengthen us through small, repeated things rather than one large event?

segments.name: Four small and simple things
steps: Divide into four groups and assign each one heading from the board. Each group reads the matching part of the talk and its scripture: scripture study with Mosiah 1:6–7; prayer with Doctrine and Covenants 88:63; the sacrament with Doctrine and Covenants 20:77, 79; covenants with the words of President Oaks that Elder Chigbundu quotes.
Give groups five minutes to discuss the two questions below. Ask one person in each group to be ready with a one-minute report.
Hear the four reports. Write one phrase from each under its heading.

If no one mentions it, point out what Elder Chigbundu says each practice does: scripture study helps us come to know the Lord; prayer draws us near to Heavenly Father; the sacrament strengthens our relationship with the Savior; covenants create a bond between us and God, and worship in the house of the Lord brings personal direction.
questions: According to Elder Chigbundu, what does this practice do for us?
When has this practice strengthened you during a hard season? What did that look like on an ordinary day?

segments.name: When the burden stays
steps: Retell the visit in Côte d'Ivoire: after a Saturday session of stake conference, Elder Chigbundu and the stake president visited a sister battling cancer. When they asked how she was feeling, she said that as she prays daily she realizes the Savior loves her and sees His hands all around her.
Read Mosiah 24:14–15 aloud, slowly. Ask learners to look for what the Lord changed and what He did not.
Read the second key quote (T11.19) and the words of President Eyring that Elder Chigbundu quotes. Add Elder Hathaway's sentence about grace as an enabling power.
Discuss the questions. Allow silence; do not rush to fill it.
questions: What is the difference between a burden removed and a back made stronger? When have you experienced the second?
Elder Chigbundu says our “Why me?” questions can be replaced by “What can I learn, and what can I change?” What helps that change of question happen?

segments.name: Choose one and begin
steps: Read both of Elder Chigbundu's invitations aloud, then the third key quote (T11.25), where he calls these four things the armor of God.
Ask learners to unfold their slip. On the back, in silence, they write one small and simple thing they will do daily this week for that burden, and when and where they will do it.
Invite them to tell the person beside them only the practice and the time, not the burden.
Point to the promise in the first key quote: strength and courage to withstand. Bear a brief testimony of the Savior's power to strengthen.
Tell the class you will begin next week by asking what they noticed. Follow through: open next week with two minutes of sharing.
questions: As a check before closing: in one sentence, what does Elder Chigbundu mean by spiritual immunity?

key_quotes.text: As we build our spiritual immunity, we develop the strength and courage to withstand the challenges of life.
The burden we carry may not always be removed, but our backs will be built to carry the load placed upon them
While they may seem small and simple, they are truly the armor of God that will help us stand against the tactics of the devil!
Our “Why me?” questions will be replaced by “What can I learn, and what can I change?”

scriptures.use: Read together in the second segment to name the principle; the words appear in the talk.
Read aloud slowly in the fourth segment; look for what the Lord changed and what He did not.
The prayer group reads it and marks what the Savior asks and what He promises.
The sacrament group reads it and lists the promises we make.

aligned_quotes.speaker: President Henry B. Eyring
aligned_quotes.text: [Proving] moments are not evidence that the Lord has abandoned you. Rather, they are evidence that He loves you enough to refine and strengthen you

aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder Hathaway
aligned_quotes.text: This grace does not remove the pain and difficulty of affliction; it is an enabling power

invitations.text: I invite you to search the scriptures diligently, that you might know the word of God
I invite you to always remember scriptures, prayers, the sacrament, and covenants.

takeaways: Spiritual immunity is built by small and simple things done daily.
The Lord may not remove my burden, but He will strengthen me to carry it.
Scriptures, prayer, the sacrament, and covenants are the armor of God.
act: Choose one of the four practices and set a fixed time and place for it each day this week.
During the sacrament this Sunday, silently ask what the Savior would have you do, and write down what comes.
When a worry returns at night, pray about it by name before doing anything else.
Set a date to worship in the house of the Lord, or take one step toward being ready to.
adapt: At home or with fewer than six people: skip the groups and take the four practices one at a time together, giving each about two minutes.
With a large class: let several groups take the same practice, and hear only one report for each heading.
If time is short: keep the opening question, the fourth segment, and the closing choice.

youth.title: Build Your Immunity
youth.big_idea: Small and simple things done daily—scripture study, prayer, the sacrament, and covenants—build spiritual immunity, giving us strength and courage through Jesus Christ to face hard things.
youth.objective: Youth will explain how one small daily practice builds spiritual strength and will commit to a seven-day plan for one practice, with a partner to check in.
prepare: Read Elder Christian C. Chigbundu's talk, Spiritual Immunity. Know the story of the new missionary well enough to tell it in your own words.
Bring paper, pens, and small slips of paper.
Label four corners of the room: Scripture study, Prayer, The sacrament, Covenants.
Ask youth to have the talk open in Gospel Library on a phone or to share with someone who does.

segments.name: Sixty-second list
steps: As soon as the prayer ends, split into two or three teams. Each team has sixty seconds to list everything a person does to keep the body able to fight off sickness. Longest list wins.
Have the winning team read its list. Ask what the items have in common. Draw out that they are small, ordinary, and repeated.
Explain that during the health crisis of 2020, Elder Chigbundu kept hearing the word immunity in health sessions at his work, and he began to think about what he calls spiritual immunity.

segments.name: What are we up against?
steps: Give each person a slip. Ask them to write, without a name, one thing that weighs on people their age. Collect the slips and read several aloud without comment.
Ask someone to read the first key quote (T11.04). Point out that Elder Chigbundu says that, frightening as our challenges may be, we need not fear.
Read Alma 37:6 together and ask the question below.
questions: Honestly, does it seem believable that small things could help with what is on those slips? Why or why not?

segments.name: Four corners
steps: Send a team to each corner. Using the talk on their phones, each team has five minutes to prepare a thirty-second case for its practice.
Each case needs three parts: one sentence from Elder Chigbundu's talk about the practice, the scripture he cites, and one real example of how it would help with something from the slips.

Scriptures for each corner: Mosiah 1:6–7 for scripture study; Doctrine and Covenants 88:63 for prayer; Doctrine and Covenants 20:77, 79 for the sacrament. The covenants corner uses the words of President Oaks that Elder Chigbundu quotes.
Hear the four cases. Thank each team by naming something specific it said well.
Sum up with Elder Chigbundu's phrase from the third key quote: these four are the armor of God.

segments.name: The missionary who wanted to go home
steps: Tell the story: when Elder Chigbundu was serving as a mission leader, a new missionary cried in his welcome interview and asked to be sent home. He could not find words to explain why. Asked whether he had a testimony of the Book of Mormon, he said he did not.

Continue: Elder Chigbundu bore his testimony and encouraged him to study the scriptures, especially the Book of Mormon. The missionary and his trainer made a scripture study plan. Later he wrote that daily study had helped him understand his purpose. Read his words in the second key quote (T11.13).
Ask the questions below. For the second one, share Elder Lebethoa's sentence and President Uchtdorf's sentence from the aligned quotes.
questions: The missionary could not explain what was wrong. When have you felt off and not known why?
What if someone reads the scriptures and does not feel anything at first? What in this story, and in these two sentences, speaks to that?

segments.name: A stronger back
steps: Read Mosiah 24:14–15 in pairs. Each pair decides: what did the Lord change, and what did He leave in place?
Read the fourth key quote (T11.19). Tell briefly of the sister in Côte d'Ivoire who is battling cancer and told Elder Chigbundu that as she prays daily she realizes the Savior loves her.
Ask the question below. Be gentle; some in the room may be carrying something that has not gone away.
questions: If the hard thing does not go away, what would it look like for the Lord to make you stronger in it?

segments.name: Seven days, one thing
steps: Read Elder Chigbundu's two invitations aloud.
Each person picks one of the four practices and writes a seven-day plan: what, what time, and where. Those with phones set a daily reminder now.
Pair up. Partners agree on a day midweek to check in with each other in person or by message.
Check understanding: ask two volunteers to finish this sentence in their own words—Spiritual immunity is…
Point to the promise in the first key quote, bear your testimony of the Savior, and say you will ask next week how the seven days went. Begin next week's class with that question.

key_quotes.text: As we build our spiritual immunity, we develop the strength and courage to withstand the challenges of life.
I am happy now and do not want to be sent home any longer.
While they may seem small and simple, they are truly the armor of God that will help us stand against the tactics of the devil!
The burden we carry may not always be removed, but our backs will be built to carry the load placed upon them

scriptures.use: Read together in the second segment, right after the slips, to state the principle; the words appear in the talk.
Read in pairs in the fifth segment; decide what the Lord changed and what He left in place.
The prayer corner reads it and uses it in its thirty-second case.
The scripture study corner reads it and finds what King Benjamin asked his sons to do.

aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder Lebethoa
aligned_quotes.text: the method, timing, and length of our scripture study matter less than the consistency and sincerity of our effort

aligned_quotes.speaker: President Uchtdorf
aligned_quotes.text: Spiritual growth is rarely dramatic at the beginning.

invitations.text: I invite you to search the scriptures diligently, that you might know the word of God
I invite you to always remember scriptures, prayers, the sacrament, and covenants.

takeaways: Spiritual strength is built by small things done every day.
The Lord may not take the hard thing away, but He will make me stronger.
Scriptures, prayer, the sacrament, and covenants are armor I can put on now.
act: Follow your seven-day plan for one practice, at the time and place you wrote down.
Check in with your partner midweek and tell the truth about how it is going.
During the sacrament on Sunday, ask silently what the Savior would have you do this week.
Like the missionary and his trainer, make a simple scripture study plan with a friend or family member.
music: As I Search the Holy Scriptures
adapt: At home or with three or four youth: skip the corners. Let each person choose one practice, find its paragraph in the talk, and teach it to the others in one minute.
With a large class: put two teams in each corner and hear the stronger case from each.
If time is short: do the sixty-second list, the missionary story, and the seven-day plan.

children.title: Little Things Make Me Strong
children.big_idea: Small and simple things, like reading the scriptures and praying every day, help me stay close to Jesus and be strong.
children.objective: Children will say that small and simple things make them strong and will choose one small thing to do each day this week.
prepare: Read Elder Christian C. Chigbundu's talk, Spiritual Immunity, especially the story of the new missionary.
Bring building blocks (or small boxes or books that stack safely).
Bring paper and crayons for each child, and a copy of the Book of Mormon.
Practice the four actions in the third segment so you can lead them without notes.

segments.name: Sing and pray
steps: Sing Scripture Power or A Child's Prayer together. Invite a child to pray.
Tell the children that today they will learn one sentence, and say it with them twice, slowly: Small and simple things make me strong.

segments.name: One block at a time
steps: Hold up one block. Ask if one block is a tall tower. Set it down.
Let the children take turns adding one block each. Each time a block goes on, everyone says: Small and simple.
When the tower is tall, ask how it got that way. Help them see it grew one small block at a time.

Explain that Elder Chigbundu, a leader in the Church, taught that small and simple things done every day help us be strong and brave when things are hard. Show Alma 37:6 in the Book of Mormon and read it aloud.
questions: What is something small you do every day that helps your body grow strong?

segments.name: Four strong things
steps: Teach four actions for the four things Elder Chigbundu named. Scriptures: hold hands open like a book. Prayer: fold arms and bow head. The sacrament: sit down quietly with a hand on the heart, thinking of Jesus. Covenants, which are promises with Heavenly Father: stand tall with arms at your sides.
Practice each one once, saying its name together.
Play the game: call out the four names in mixed order, slowly at first and then faster, while the children do the actions.
End with everyone standing tall. Say the sentence together: Small and simple things make me strong.

segments.name: The missionary and the scriptures
steps: Tell the story simply: Elder Chigbundu was a mission leader. A new missionary came. He was so sad that he cried, and he asked to go home.

Continue: Elder Chigbundu told him he knew the Book of Mormon is true and asked him to study the scriptures. The missionary and his companion made a plan to study every day. Later the missionary wrote a letter. Read his words from the first key quote (T11.13).
Act it out together: make a sad face; open pretend scriptures and read while counting seven days aloud, marching in place; pretend to write a letter; show a happy face.
Ask the questions below.
questions: What small thing did the missionary do every day?
How did he feel after he kept doing it?

segments.name: Draw my small and simple thing
steps: Tell the children that Elder Chigbundu also taught that when we pray, we come close to Heavenly Father. He met a sister who was sick. She told him that as she prayed every day, she knew that the Savior loves her.

Give each child paper and crayons. Ask them to draw themselves doing one small and simple thing: reading the scriptures, praying, thinking of Jesus during the sacrament, or keeping a promise to Heavenly Father.
Walk around and ask each child to tell you about the drawing. Write the child's words at the bottom if they would like.

segments.name: Choose and share
steps: Sit in a circle. Each child holds up the drawing and finishes this sentence: This week, every day, I will…
Explain that Elder Chigbundu invited everyone to always remember scriptures, prayers, the sacrament, and covenants, and taught that these help us be strong and brave.
Say the sentence together one last time, starting in a whisper and ending in a clear, happy voice.
Share your testimony in two or three sentences that Heavenly Father and Jesus Christ love each child.
Send the drawings home. Next week, begin by asking who did their small thing and how it felt.

key_quotes.text: I am happy now and do not want to be sent home any longer.
By small and simple things are great things brought to pass
When we pray to our Heavenly Father, we draw near to Him and seek His help, guidance, and blessings.

scriptures.use: Show the verse in the Book of Mormon after the block tower and read it aloud; the words appear in the talk.
With older children, read it before drawing and ask what Jesus promises when we come close to Him.

aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder Morgan
aligned_quotes.text: No time or effort is ever wasted in reading the Book of Mormon.

invitations.text: I invite you to always remember scriptures, prayers, the sacrament, and covenants.

takeaways: Small and simple things make me strong.
When I pray, I come close to Heavenly Father.
Jesus loves me and helps me.
act: Do the small thing in your drawing every day this week.
Put your drawing where you will see it each morning.
Tell someone at home the sentence you learned and show them the four actions.

adapt.younger: For ages 3–7: keep the story to four sentences and act it out twice. Use only two actions, scriptures and prayer, in the game. Let each child place a block with a helper and repeat the sentence after every activity. They may draw only themselves praying.
adapt.older: For ages 8–11: have a child read Alma 37:6 and another read Doctrine and Covenants 88:63 aloud. Let an older child lead the four-actions game. Ask a harder question: Why do you think Heavenly Father helps us through small things we do every day instead of one big thing? You may share Elder Morgan's sentence about reading the Book of Mormon.
